2 Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, on the authority of Ḥumrān.

3 Therefore, there is no need for another cause to bestow existence upon existence

These two states also apply to our external actions. As long as we are not about to perform any act, any given action wavers between being performed and not being performed. If its causes and conditions come together, and if they are completed by our will and determination, there will be nothing lefiifor it but to occur. In this case, one of the two possibilities is determined for it: occurrence.

The same two states apply to our conventional affairs and ascriptions. For instance, when two people dispute over to whom something belongs, its ownership wavers between the two individuals. Then, when they go to a judge to settle their dispute and he rules in favor of one of them, this rule severs the matter from ambiguity and uncertainty; it determines and establishes the connection of the object to one of the two individuals and disconnects it from the other.

This is an extension on the meaning of qaḍāʾ because it assumes a verbal judgment and determination to be similar to judgment and determination of actions. Hence when the judge says that the property belongs to one

of the two litigants, his words serve as a decisive judgment for the dispute and the determination of one of the two sides after their state of uncertainty. Likewise, when someone says, “x is y,” this is a decisive judgment

(faṣl) and determination (taʿyīn), and this is what we call decree (qaḍāʾ). Since the existence and realization of all events are attributable to God as His actions, the two considerations apply there as well: As long as God has not willed the occurrence of an event and as long as its necessary causes and conditions are incomplete, it remains wavering between

occurrence and non-occurrence. But once God has willed its happening and completes its causes and all conditions, nothing is lefiifor it but to be brought into existence. This is God’s determination (taʿyīn) of one side for the event, and its severance (faṣl) from the other side, which removes the ambiguity. This is called a decree by God.

These two considerations apply in a like manner to the plane of legislation (tashrīʿ). His decisive command and ruling about something is a

decree (qaḍāʾ) by Him.

His existential (takwīnī) decree is seen in many verses such as:

And when He decrees (qaḍā) an affair, He only says to it, Be, so there it is. (2:117);

So He ordained them (qaḍāhunn) seven heavens in two periods. (41:12); itself. (Trans.)

The matter is decreed (qaḍā) concerning which you inquired. (12:41); And We had made known (wa qaḍaynā) to the children of Israel in the Book: Most certainly you will make mischief in the land twice. (17:4) Examples of verses addressing legislative decree are:

And your Lord has commanded (qaḍā) that you shall not serve (any)

but Him, and goodness to your parents. (17:23)

Surely your Lord will judge (yaqḍī) between them on the resurrection day concerning that in which they disagreed. (10:93)

And judgment shall be given between them with justice, and it shall be said: All praise is due to Allah, the Lord of the worlds. (39:75)

Decree in this last verse and the verses before it [in Chapter 39] is legislative settlement of disputes in one respect, and existential decree in another.

These noble verses, as you can see, confirm the two senses of God’s qaḍāʾ (decree, judgment): It is applied to existential things as they are God’s [cosmic and creative] acts, and to the divine legislations as they are His legislative acts. The same is true about decisive judgment attributed to Him.

This decree is sometimes referred to as ḥukm (judgment) and sometimes as qawl (speech, word). He says:

Now surely His is the judgment (al-ḥukm). (6:62)

And Allah pronounces a doom (yaḥkumu)—there is no repeller of His decree (li-ḥukmihi). (13:41)

My word shall not be changed. (50:29)

And the truth do I speak (aqūlu, from qawl). (38:84)

A Philosophical View Concerning Decree

There is no doubt that the law of cause and effect is correct and that a contingent existent is an effect of God either directly or through an intermediary. If we consider an effect along with its ascription to its complete

cause, then it derives necessity [of existence] from its complete cause. This is because as long as [the existence of] something is not necessitated, it does not exist.1 But if we consider an effect by itself and irrespective of its complete cause, then it will be contingent. Thus is the case whether it is

1 This is based on the above discussion, that the complete cause determines existence for the effect over non-existence. Therefore, assuming the presence of the complete cuase, the effect would be characterized by necessity of existence. (Trans).

looked at in isolation and unlinked to anything, such as contingent quiddities per se; or it is considered along with some of its complete cause.

Either way it will be contingent, because if it is necessary, it would mean that its cause is complete, while the premise is the opposite.

Necessity means the determination of one side [that is, either existence or non-existence], which puts an end to the state of uncertainty

of an event. Thus, if we consider the entire chain of contingent beings with regard to its link to the Necessary Being, then each contingent being derives necessity from Him within its specific container [of time and place, or existential plane]. This general necessity that encompasses the chain of contingent beings is a universal decree by Him, just as the necessity specific to each of them is a particular decree by Him, for by decree we mean nothing but the determination of one of the two sides, as opposed to a state of indetermination and uncertainty.

This shows that decree (qaḍāʾ) is an attribute of divine actions (al-ṣifāt al-fiʿliyyah). It is derived from an act’s (fiʿl) relationship with its complete cause that necessitates it.

Another Philosophical Discussion

Based on verse 17:20 (and the bounty of your Lord is not confined), it can be inferred that God’s effusion is unconditional and unlimited. Rational arguments are all unanimous that the existence of the Necessary Being is absolute, for it is inherently necessary. His existence is not delimited by any limit, restricted by any restriction, or conditional upon any condition. Otherwise it means that it does not exist beyond its limit, and would totally be lost with the absence of its condition. Given that He is inherently necessary,2 He must be One—such one that has no conceivable second to it. Also, He must be Absolute—such absolute that would never take any condition.

Furthermore, it has been proven that the existence of everything else is an effect worked by Him. We also know that an act is necessarily congruous to its doer. Hence, the effect issuing from Him is also one—a true

one that reflects the Ultimate One (waḥdat ḥaqqah ẓilliyyah). His act must also be absolute and unlimited; otherwise, His Essence would be composed of two things: 1) a limit; and 2) what takes the limit. In other words, His Essence would be composed of existence and non-existence. The essential dichotomy between these two [that is, existence and non-existence] would apply to the Doer’s Essence as there must be some congruence between the Doer and His deed. However, this is against the original premise that He is absolutely One. Therefore existence, which is His act and effect, is also one and not many, absolute and not limited.

It then follows that the differences of the contingent beings which

The preparatory cause (al-ʿillat al-muʿiddah) has a single absolute effusion. However, the receptacles are many according to their different receiving capacities. There are some receptacles that do not accept the effusion at all, but embrace the exact opposite [of that effusion]. There are other receptacles that fully accept the effusion, and there are those [in between] that receive the effusion partially and convert it to a form that matches their particular potentiality. It is like the sun which radiates one light with uniform parts, but then the bodies receiving its light dispose of it according to their capacity and potentiality.

You might object that undoubtedly these differences are real. If the quiddities and capacities deemed to be the root of them are illusory and unreal matters, it makes no sense to attribute these real things to them. Thus, these differences would go back to existence which is the effect of the True Creator. This, however, contradicts the claim that God’s effusion is unconditional. And if those quiddities and capacities are also

So again these differences would be attributable to God’s act [of effusion],2 which contradicts the above claim [of absoluteness of God’s effusion].

The answer to this is: Our view above defines all different existents to be of the same single reality of existence, which leaves no room for any

In other words, dividing absolute existent into quiddity and existence, or into potentiality and actuality, is what has brought about negations [that is, non-existence, due to demarcations] in reality. It is thus that things are classified into haves and have nots, perfect and deprived, receptacle and effusion. The source of these classifications is the mental analysis of things into:

(1) quiddity, which is receptive to existence; and (2) existence, which is received by quiddity.

Likewise is the analysis of things into:

(1) potentialities that lack actuality; and (2) actualities that oppose potentiality. But if we retrace all things to the single absolute reality of existence [instead of mentally decomposing them], there would be no room to discuss the cause of differences. In that case, the Creator’s effect—that is, effusion—would be absolutely one with no multiplicity or limit to

it. Contemplate this!
